title: Mardana's last song
hookLine: tradition says when Mardana died, Nanak asked his son Shahzada to carry on playing
tomorrow: The boy who feared the fire

lines: A GUITAR CASE BY THE DOOR.
cards: A guitar case sits by the door after the funeral. Nobody wants to open it. Everybody knows what's inside: the strings he tuned, the pick still tucked under them.
Somebody, someday, has to decide what happens to it. All along this path, when Nanak sang, a rabab played beside him, in the hands of Mardana, the Muslim musician who walked the long roads with him.
He was there at the strange cities, the hunger, the bitter fruit. Today the music changes hands.

teach.b: Tellings disagree about where Mardana died. Some place it on the road, far to the west; some at Kartarpur, near the end of Nanak's travels. What they share is the shape.

Tradition says that as Mardana grew weak, Nanak sat with him and asked what he wished for his body: did he want a tomb raised over him, as was done for honored men? And Mardana, the story goes, said no.

Why trap me in a tomb of stone, when you've freed me from the tomb of the body? In some tellings, Nanak and his Sikhs then sang hymns for him, and Nanak told the family not to wail but to sing the Lord's praise.
Tradition says Nanak called Mardana's son, Shahzada, and asked him to take up the rabab and keep playing.
Look at what this ending keeps: a friendship that never asked Mardana to stop being who he was, a Muslim musician and a Guru, side by side to the end. And what doesn't get built: no monument.

Sikh tradition remembers rababis, rabab players descended from Mardana, playing kirtan in the courts of later Gurus. Grief can make the music stop. In this story, the comfort Nanak gives is a job: pick it up, and play.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rabab player, and the rabab and the rababi tradition of kirtan are honored in Sikh music.

games.q: your oldest friend, a musician, has died. his son stands holding the instrument, not knowing what to do. what do you say?
o: put it away; it's too painful now.
build a monument and hang it there.
take it up and keep playing.
games.why: tradition says Nanak asked Shahzada to carry on playing. the memorial was the music, not a tomb.

practice: Let one musician come to mind: a singer who carried you through a hard year, whoever leads the hymns where you worship, a grandparent who hummed while cooking, a kid down the street learning trumpet badly and bravely.
Let the sound come back to you, and quietly thank them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.
